Appropriate policy and legislative reforms will accommodate the functional aspects of a digital currency. The draft Central Bank of The Bahamas Bill, 2019, now before the Government, anticipates this framework, and will provide for the development of regulations to govern the instrument. The regulatory framework will include safeguards to satisfy Exchange Control Regulations; monitoring and controls against money laundering and terrorist financing, and specifications to ensure complementarity as opposed to material substitutability for existing banking services. This initiative has acquired the name Project Sand Dollar, with the sand dollar also being the name assigned to the proposed central bank digital currency (CBDC). This is a continuation of the Bahamian Payments System Modernization Initiative (PSMI), which began in the early 2000s. The Bahamian PSMI targets improved outcomes for financial inclusion and access, making the domestic payments system more efficient and non-discriminatory in access to financial services. Although average measures of financial development and access in The Bahamas are high by international standards, pockets of the population are excluded because of the remoteness of some communities outside of the cost effective reach of physical banking services. More onerous customer due diligence standards for AML/CFT international tax compliance have also resulted in forms of exclusion, including more recent responses to tighter "know your customer" (KYC) systems introduced to preserve international correspondent banking relationships. As recent policy and regulatory reforms have begun to tackle these barriers, the Central Bank is intent on accelerating payments system reform, admitting new categories of financial services providers and using the digital payments infrastructure to make the supply of traditional banking services accessible to all segments of the population. Belle Research Department Central Bank of The Bahamas July 26, 2022 1 Introduction The global payments landscape continues to evolve as advancements in the field are being made through globalization and digitization. These develop- ments have resulted in increased interest in the implementation of central bank digital currencies, hereafter CBDC, among policy makers and other interest groups. The Bahamas is considered a global leader in CBDC de- velopment following the launch of its CBDC, Sand Dollar, in October 2020. It is the first country in the region and among the few globally, to launch a central bank digital currency. The use of a CBDC would offer another method of payment as not all consumers have credit or debit cards. Providing a safe and liquid government- backed means of completing payments without the necessity of getting or The views expressed in this paper do not represent those of the Central Bank of The Bahamas. For internal circulation only. 1 Wright, Belle, McKenzie, Bodie: Financial Inclusion & CBDC maintaining a bank account. The goal of Sand Dollar is to advance more inclusive access to regulated payments and other financial services for under- serviced communities and socio-economic groups, as well as reduce ser- vice delivery costs and increase transactional efficiency for financial services across The Bahamas (Central Bank of The Bahamas, 2020). The purpose of this research memo is to assess the extent to which the Sand Dollar is capable of achieving these goals. The purpose of this paper is to develop a dynamic, stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model of CBDC adoption in The Bahamas. The model allows us to assess how CBDC adoption will impact monetary and fiscal policy and is a Two-Agent, New Keynesian (TANK) Model first developed by Bilbiie (2008) with open-economy features, critical for the assessment in countries like The Bahamas. The TANK framework has become a standard model for assessing monetary policy when households are unbanked. We interpret Non-Savers as those who gain access to financial services through CBDC. Thus, our analysis focuses on a careful calibration of this impor- tant parameter. We discuss the model in detail below. To highlight a few important results: If the adoption rate of CBDC is sufficiently high, then 1. the volatility pass-through of monetary policy shocks falls substan- tially. 2. variance decompositions show that technology shocks account for the lion's share of volatility in the model. 3. negative monetary policy feedback effects are mitigated. 4. recessionary shocks are less likely. 5. Welfare of households, especially the constrained households, improves. Our analysis depends critically on the fraction of households who do not have access to financial services that would gain access over the course of the next several years. Our estimate of 70k persons or 17.9% of popula- tion (IMF, 2019) that remains unbanked is discussed in detail below. The primary goal of the Sand Dollar project is to provide financial services to 2 Wright, Belle, McKenzie, Bodie: Financial Inclusion & CBDC those not currently integrated in the Bahamian banking system. If the Sand Dollar cuts the number of unbanked in half, the economic benefits discussed above come to fruition. The intuition of these results comes from the in- terest rate channel of monetary policy. If the population is 100% banked, then monetary policy can fully control inflation. The volatility of monetary policy pass-through is tied specifically to the number of unbanked. As this number increases, monetary policy loses control of inflation dynamics. This main mechanism spills over into the impact of monetary policy on the real economy. If there is a substantial number of unbanked, variance decompo- sitions show that monetary policy has a much more significant impact on the volatility of GDP. As the number of unbanked falls, technology shocks account for the lion's share of volatility in the model. Thus, policy mistakes are amplified as the number of unbanked increases. 1.1 Stylized Facts on CBDC Adoption The success of any CBDC and its potential impact on economic growth are dependent upon the rate of adoption by consumers and businesses. Mini-report on how the Bahamas CBDC pilot was implemented

The Bahamas CBDC pilot, known as Project Sand Dollar, was launched as a payments-system modernization initiative with a clear phased rollout. The official launch announcement states that the pilot began in Exuma in December 2019 and was planned to extend to Abaco in the first half of 2020 [N1-F2]. A later official source notes that the pilot phase was followed by a gradual national release in mid-October 2020, after which Sand Dollar moved from pilot to production [N6-R5]. This timeline supports the conclusion that the pilot was not a one-off experiment but part of a longer rollout strategy.

On scope and target population, the pilot was designed to test the digital currency in a specific geographic context that would later inform a national rollout. The Bahamian Central Bank described Exuma as a microcosm of the country and emphasized that the initiative was intended to improve access to financial services in areas outside the cost-effective reach of physical banking services [N1-F2]. The bank also noted that average financial development and access in The Bahamas were already high by international standards, but pockets of the population remained excluded due to remoteness and more onerous customer due diligence standards [N1-F2]. This means the pilot was targeted at communities that are geographically difficult to serve and that face exclusion from financial services because of remoteness and compliance burdens [N1-F2].

The technical architecture and distribution mechanism were described as a digital fiat currency system built on a payments infrastructure modernization plan. The official announcement states that the Central Bank selected NZIA Limited as the preferred technology solutions provider, with IBM and Zynesis Pte Ltd contributing blockchain expertise [N1-F1]. The project’s document also highlights automated clearing arrangements, non-bank direct participation in settlements, and strengthening ease of access to financial services as key components of the infrastructure [N1-F2]. The distribution mechanism appears to be centered on a digital wallet-based system, with the central bank emphasizing equal, expanded access to modernized digital payments capabilities [N1-F1]. The implementation plan also included an education and marketing strategy, indicating that the CBDC was intended to be deployed alongside user awareness campaigns [N1-F2].

For regulatory approvals and collaboration with local partners, the Bahamian authorities framed the project within a broader legal and policy context. The 2019 draft Central Bank of the Bahamas Bill anticipated the framework for developing regulations to govern the instrument and included safeguards for exchange control, money laundering, terrorist financing, and complementarity with existing banking services [N1-F1]. The legal framework page also notes that the Central Bank of the Bahamas provides links to relevant legislation and that the Bahamian Dollar Digital Currency Regulations 2021 and related acts were available through official channels [N2-F3]. In terms of collaboration, the project was explicitly partnered with NZIA Limited, which brought together IBM and Zynesis Pte Ltd, and the Central Bank also worked with local financial-service providers and other stakeholders as part of its payments-system modernization plan [N1-F2]. The emphasis on stakeholder roles and contribution indicates that the implementation relied on both internal central-bank capacity and external technology and financial-service partners [N1-F2].

Overall, the pilot was implemented as a controlled, phased test of a digital currency system in a remote island setting, with a clear plan for national expansion, a technology partnership centered on blockchain and payments infrastructure, and a regulatory framework that balanced innovation with safeguards and stakeholder collaboration [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-F3].

Mini-report on the project’s justification for financial inclusion

The project’s justification for financial inclusion is explicit and centered on expanding access to regulated payments and other financial services for underserved communities. The official Bahamian paper states that the goal of Sand Dollar is “to advance more inclusive access to regulated payments and other financial services for under-serviced communities and socio-economic groups” [N3-F4]. It also states that the primary goal is to provide financial services to those not currently integrated in the Bahamian banking system [N3-F4]. This framing directly links the CBDC to improving access for populations that are excluded from formal financial services [N3-F4].

The project is also explicitly tied to remote-area access. The Central Bank’s 2019 pilot announcement noted that the initiative was intended to improve outcomes for financial inclusion and access, with the Bahamian payments system modernization targeting “improved outcomes for financial inclusion and access” and “making the domestic payments system more efficient and non-discriminatory in access to financial services” [N1-F2]. The official paper further explains that some communities are excluded because of remoteness and because more onerous customer due diligence standards have resulted in forms of exclusion [N1-F2]. It also says that recent policy and regulatory reforms have begun to tackle these barriers, and the Central Bank is accelerating payments-system reform to make traditional banking services accessible to all segments of the population [N1-F2]. This means the project is justified not just as a payment innovation but as a means to address structural exclusion in remote and underserved areas [N1-F2].

The pilot is expected to reduce exclusion from payments and services by providing a safe, liquid, government-backed means of completing payments without the necessity of having a bank account [N3-F4]. The official paper emphasizes that the CBDC would offer another method of payment for people who do not have credit or debit cards [N3-F4]. It also highlights that the goal is to reduce service delivery costs and increase transactional efficiency for financial services across The Bahamas [N1-F1]. These statements imply that the project is designed to lower barriers to participation in the financial system, especially for those who are excluded by the cost of physical banking or by the need for formal account access [N1-F1][N3-F4].

Evidence or statements about cost, convenience, and trust are mixed. The project explicitly states that the CBDC is expected to reduce the ill effects of cash usage and reduce transactions costs [N1-F2]. It also describes the digital payment process as convenient, secure, and cost-effective, and notes that the digital currency experience is tailored to users [N1-F2]. The official paper also notes that the Central Bank expects that at the conclusion of the project, all residents will have equal, expanded access to modernized digital payments capabilities [N1-F1]. This suggests that convenience and accessibility are central to the inclusion rationale [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Trust is implied by the emphasis on safety, liquidity, and government backing [N3-F4]. However, the evidence provided here does not include direct survey data on user trust levels or broad adoption confidence beyond the stated objectives [N3-F4]. So while the justification is strong on cost and convenience, the evidence for trust is more implicit than quantified [N3-F4][N1-F2].

Mini-report on broader CBDC and financial inclusion context

Common CBDC arguments for financial inclusion are well established in the evidence. The IMF paper notes that CBDC has special aspects that may benefit financial inclusion, such as being a risk-free and widely acceptable form of digital money, and availability for offline use [N4-R1]. Another IMF source states that some central banks issue or explore retail CBDC to increase financial inclusion and enhance end-user access to central bank money [N4-R4]. A general CBDC paper likewise argues that CBDCs can contribute to financial inclusion but stresses that they cannot solve its root causes [N4-R3]. These sources show that the common CBDC rationale is that the currency can serve as a universal, secure, and accessible digital money form that reaches people who are excluded from traditional banking systems [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R3].

Where CBDC claims are supported by evidence versus speculation is an important distinction. The evidence here supports the claim that CBDC can be useful for inclusion when it is designed as a retail or near-retail instrument that lowers barriers to entry and can be used in offline settings [N4-R1][N4-R4]. It also supports the claim that CBDC can reduce transaction costs and improve access to payments, especially in countries where cash is still widely used or where formal banking access is limited [N4-R1][N4-R4]. However, the evidence also makes clear that CBDC alone is not sufficient to solve the deeper structural causes of exclusion, such as poverty, education, and infrastructure gaps [N4-R3]. In other words, CBDC is plausible as a tool for inclusion, but its impact depends on complementary reforms and is not guaranteed without them [N4-R3].

How remote-area access compares with other inclusion strategies depends on the evidence context. The Bahamas example shows that remote-area access is a major motivation for CBDC because some communities are outside the cost-effective reach of physical banking services and are excluded by remoteness and compliance burdens [N1-F2]. The broader evidence also suggests that mobile money and other digital financial services can help open access to banking in remote communities [N5-R2]. In the Caribbean context, 58% of the population in some countries have access to mobile phones, making them ideal candidates for mobile financial services and simple value transfer [N5-R5]. These points indicate that remote-area access is often addressed by digital infrastructure rather than only by CBDC. Mobile money and agency banking are also mentioned as alternative strategies [N5-R4]. The Bahamian CBDC rationale is therefore best understood as one part of a broader set of digital-inclusion strategies, rather than the only one [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

Overall, the broader CBDC context supports the inclusion argument but also limits it. CBDC can improve access, reduce costs, and increase convenience, especially for remote users [N4-R1][N4-R4]. However, the evidence here is more supportive of the inclusion rationale than it is of a universal claim that CBDC automatically solves financial exclusion [N4-R3]. Remote-area access is a strong justification for CBDC, but it is also comparable with other digital strategies such as mobile money and agency banking, meaning that CBDC should be seen as one tool among several [N1-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

# How the Central Bank of the Bahamas implemented its digital currency pilot and how it justifies the project in terms of enhancing financial inclusion, especially in remote areas

## 1) Implementation of the Bahamas CBDC pilot

The Central Bank of the Bahamas implemented its digital currency pilot as **Project Sand Dollar**, a payments-system modernization initiative with a clear phased rollout. The pilot began in **Exuma in December 2019** and was planned to extend to **Abaco in the first half of 2020** [N1-F2]. A later official source notes that the Sand Dollar pilot was followed by a **gradual national release in mid-October 2020**, after which it moved from pilot to production [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The project was also described as a continuation of the **Bahamian Payments System Modernization Initiative**, indicating that the pilot was only the first step in a broader modernization program [N1-F2].

The target population and scope of the pilot were explicitly focused on communities that are **geographically difficult to serve and excluded by remoteness and compliance burdens**. The Central Bank explained that although average financial development and access in The Bahamas were already high by international standards, pockets of the population remained excluded because of remoteness and more onerous customer due diligence standards [N1-F2]. This means the pilot was designed to test the digital currency in a setting where access to physical banking is less cost-effective and where formal financial inclusion is harder to achieve [N1-F2].

The technical architecture and distribution mechanism were centered on a **digital fiat currency system** built on a payments infrastructure modernization plan. The Central Bank selected **NZIA Limited** as the preferred technology solutions provider, with **IBM** and **Zynesis Pte Ltd** contributing blockchain expertise [N1-F1]. The project document also highlights **automated clearing arrangements**, **non-bank direct participation in settlements**, and **strengthening ease of access to financial services** as key components of the infrastructure [N1-F2]. The distribution mechanism appears to be centered on a **digital wallet-based system**, with the Central Bank emphasizing **equal, expanded access to modernized digital payments capabilities** [N1-F1]. The implementation plan also included an **education and marketing strategy**, indicating that the CBDC was intended to be deployed alongside user awareness campaigns [N1-F2].

For regulatory approvals and collaboration with local partners, the Bahamian authorities framed the project within a broader legal and policy context. The **2019 draft Central Bank of the Bahamas Bill** anticipated the framework for developing regulations to govern the instrument and included safeguards for exchange control, money laundering, terrorist financing, and complementarity with existing banking services [N1-F1]. The official legal framework page notes that the Central Bank provides links to relevant legislation and that **Bahamian Dollar Digital Currency Regulations 2021** and related acts were available through official channels [N2-F3]. In terms of collaboration, the project was explicitly partnered with **NZIA Limited**, and the Central Bank worked with local financial-service providers and other stakeholders as part of its payments-system modernization plan [N1-F2]. This indicates that the implementation relied on both internal central-bank capacity and external technology and financial-service partners [N1-F2].

## 2) Timeline, expansion, and operational rollout

The pilot’s timeline is clearly phased. It started in **Exuma in December 2019**, then expanded to **Abaco in the first half of 2020**, and then moved into a **gradual national release in mid-October 2020** [N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Another source notes that the pilot started in December 2019 after more than three years of research and planning [N6-R4]. This long lead-in supports the idea that the project was not a sudden experiment but a carefully planned modernization effort [N6-R4].

The pilot expanded beyond the initial test phase through a **national rollout** and later through a **government expenditure phase**. The official announcement says that the Sand Dollar was on schedule for a **gradual national release in mid-October 2020** [N6-R1]. A later Facebook post from July 2021 mentions **“phase two,”** which involved **government expenditure payouts in Sand Dollars throughout the cash districts of the Southern Bahamas** [N6-R3]. This indicates that the project expanded from a user-test phase into a practical operational phase focused on government payments and broader circulation [N6-R3]. Taken together, the expansion was from a single island to a second island, then to a national rollout, and then to government expenditure use [N1-F2][N6-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3].

The evidence also suggests that the rollout required careful planning and stakeholder coordination. The project document emphasizes that the Central Bank expects **appropriate policy and legislative reforms** to accommodate the functional aspects of a digital currency, and that the draft 2019 bill anticipated the framework [N1-F1]. It also notes that the project included an **education and marketing strategy** to recruit test users and that information campaigns are important for recruitment [N1-F2][N2-R2]. These points suggest that the rollout was planned with awareness and regulatory readiness in mind, rather than being a simple roll-out without safeguards [N1-F2][N2-R2]. The evidence does not provide direct accounts of major technical or operational failures, so the lessons learned are mainly implicit: the project required legal reform, stakeholder collaboration, and user education to succeed [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R2].

## 3) Justification for financial inclusion

The project’s justification for financial inclusion is explicit and centered on expanding access to regulated payments and other financial services for **under-serviced communities and socio-economic groups**. The official Bahamian paper states that the goal of Sand Dollar is “to advance more inclusive access to regulated payments and other financial services for under-serviced communities and socio-economic groups” [N3-F4]. It also states that the primary goal is to provide financial services to those not currently integrated in the Bahamian banking system [N3-F4]. This framing directly links the CBDC to improving access for populations that are excluded from formal financial services [N3-F4].

The project is also explicitly tied to **remote-area access**. The Central Bank’s 2019 pilot announcement noted that the initiative was intended to improve outcomes for financial inclusion and access, with the Bahamian payments system modernization targeting “improved outcomes for financial inclusion and access” and “making the domestic payments system more efficient and non-discriminatory in access to financial services” [N1-F2]. The official paper further explains that some communities are excluded because of remoteness and because more onerous customer due diligence standards have resulted in forms of exclusion [N1-F2]. It also says that recent policy and regulatory reforms have begun to tackle these barriers, and the Central Bank is accelerating payments-system reform to make traditional banking services accessible to all segments of the population [N1-F2]. This means the project is justified not just as a payment innovation but as a means to address structural exclusion in remote and underserved areas [N1-F2].

The pilot is expected to reduce exclusion from payments and services by providing a **safe, liquid, government-backed means of completing payments without the necessity of having a bank account** [N3-F4]. The official paper emphasizes that the CBDC would offer another method of payment for people who do not have credit or debit cards [N3-F4]. It also highlights that the goal is to reduce service delivery costs and increase transactional efficiency for financial services across The Bahamas [N1-F1]. These statements imply that the project is designed to lower barriers to participation in the financial system, especially for those who are excluded by the cost of physical banking or by the need for formal account access [N1-F1][N3-F4].

Evidence or statements about **cost, convenience, and trust** are mixed. The project explicitly states that the CBDC is expected to reduce the ill effects of cash usage and reduce transaction costs [N1-F2]. It also describes the digital payment process as **convenient, secure, and cost-effective**, and notes that the digital currency experience is tailored to users [N1-F2]. The official paper also notes that the Central Bank expects that at the conclusion of the project, all residents will have equal, expanded access to modernized digital payments capabilities [N1-F1]. This suggests that convenience and accessibility are central to the inclusion rationale [N1-F1][N1-F2]. Trust is implied by the emphasis on safety, liquidity, and government backing [N3-F4]. However, the evidence provided here does not include direct survey data on user trust levels or broad adoption confidence beyond the stated objectives [N3-F4]. So while the justification is strong on cost and convenience, the evidence for trust is more implicit than quantified [N3-F4][N1-F2].

## 4) Broader CBDC and financial inclusion context

The broader CBDC context supports the inclusion argument, but it also limits it. Common CBDC arguments for financial inclusion are that CBDC can be a **risk-free and widely acceptable form of digital money**, and that it can be **available for offline use** [N4-R1]. Another source states that some central banks issue or explore retail CBDC to increase financial inclusion and enhance end-user access to central bank money [N4-R4]. A general CBDC paper likewise argues that CBDCs can contribute to financial inclusion but stresses that they cannot solve its root causes [N4-R3]. These sources show that the common CBDC rationale is that the currency can serve as a universal, secure, and accessible digital money form that reaches people who are excluded from traditional banking systems [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R3].

Where CBDC claims are supported by evidence versus speculation is an important distinction. The evidence here supports the claim that CBDC can be useful for inclusion when it is designed as a retail or near-retail instrument that lowers barriers to entry and can be used in offline settings [N4-R1][N4-R4]. It also supports the claim that CBDC can reduce transaction costs and improve access to payments, especially in countries where cash is still widely used or where formal banking access is limited [N4-R1][N4-R4]. However, the evidence also makes clear that CBDC alone is not sufficient to solve the deeper structural causes of exclusion, such as poverty, education, and infrastructure gaps [N4-R3]. In other words, CBDC is plausible as a tool for inclusion, but its impact depends on complementary reforms and is not guaranteed without them [N4-R3].

How remote-area access compares with other inclusion strategies depends on the evidence context. The Bahamas example shows that remote-area access is a major motivation for CBDC because some communities are outside the cost-effective reach of physical banking services and are excluded by remoteness and compliance burdens [N1-F2]. The broader evidence also suggests that **mobile money and other digital financial services can help open access to banking in remote communities** [N5-R2]. In the Caribbean context, 58% of the population in some countries have access to mobile phones, making them ideal candidates for mobile financial services and simple value transfer [N5-R5]. These points indicate that remote-area access is often addressed by digital infrastructure rather than only by CBDC. **Agency banking** is also mentioned as an alternative strategy [N5-R4]. The Bahamian CBDC rationale is therefore best understood as one part of a broader set of digital-inclusion strategies, rather than the only one [N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5].

## 5) Bottom line

In short, the Central Bank of the Bahamas implemented its digital currency pilot through a phased, stakeholder-driven approach: launching in **Exuma in December 2019**, expanding to **Abaco in 2020**, and then rolling out nationally in **mid-October 2020** [N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The pilot was designed to test a **digital fiat currency system** built on a payments infrastructure modernization plan, with a digital wallet-based distribution mechanism and collaboration with **NZIA Limited**, **IBM**, and **Zynesis Pte Ltd** [N1-F1]. Regulatory support came from the **2019 draft Central Bank of the Bahamas Bill** and related legislation, showing the project was embedded in a legal framework that balanced innovation with safeguards [N1-F1][N2-F3].

The justification for the project is centered on **enhancing financial inclusion**, especially in **remote areas**. The Central Bank explicitly claims that Sand Dollar will advance more inclusive access to regulated payments and other financial services for **under-serviced communities and socio-economic groups** [N3-F4]. It also frames the project as addressing exclusion caused by **remoteness and compliance burdens**, and as a way to make traditional banking services accessible to all segments of the population [N1-F2]. The project is expected to reduce exclusion by providing a **safe, liquid, government-backed means of completing payments** without the need for a bank account [N3-F4], while also reducing **transaction costs** and improving **transactional efficiency** [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports the inclusion rationale, especially for remote areas, but it also shows that CBDC is one tool among several. It can improve **access, cost, and convenience**, but it does not automatically solve deeper structural issues [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R3]. In the Bahamian case, the CBDC pilot is best understood as a modernization effort aimed at improving access for underserved communities while relying on legal reform, stakeholder collaboration, and user education to succeed [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R2].
